articles.title: A $100 billion “ghost city” became a home for tech entrepreneurs, but the experiment lasted less than two years after it began
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Forest City was meant to become a futuristic metropolis near Singapore, but its empty towers and quiet streets earned it a very different reputation. .
articles.body: Forest City was meant to become a futuristic metropolis near Singapore, but its empty towers and quiet streets earned it a very different reputation. That unusual setting later attracted a group of technology entrepreneurs who saw the underused development as an opportunity to test a new way of living and working. In 2024, Network School arrived with a community built around technology, startups and the ideas of Balaji Srinivasan’s The Network State. Participants lived, worked and learned together inside the development. Yet the experiment faced practical problems, including living conditions, licensing issues and scrutiny from Malaysian authorities. Less than two years after it began, Network School was ordered to cease operations.How Forest City’s ghost-town reputation helped attract a new technology communityForest City was conceived as an enormous mixed-use development in Johor, close to the Singapore border. The project included high-rise residential buildings, hotels, retail areas and recreational facilities, with plans originally aimed at accommodating hundreds of thousands of people. According to the BBC, around $100 billion has been associated with the development over the years.Large parts of the development remained underoccupied, giving Forest City its reputation as a ghost town. The Covid-19 pandemic made the situation harder, while wider problems affecting China's property sector added to the difficulties facing the project. Streets and apartment blocks existed, but there were not enough people using them to create the ordinary bustle associated with a major urban centre.Srinivasan’s Network State idea became a real-world experiment in Forest CitySrinivasan had been developing his thinking about alternative communities for years before arriving in Forest City.His 2022 book, The Network State, proposed a model in which people could first gather digitally around shared interests and beliefs, build businesses and financial relationships, acquire physical territory and eventually seek some form of political recognition.Srinivasan, a former Coinbase chief technology officer who had also worked in venture capital and co-founded genomics company Counsyl, had spent much of his career around technology and startups. The school was not simply intended as a conventional educational programme. It combined accommodation, work space, classes, fitness and communal activities, giving participants the chance to live together while developing companies and pursuing projects.According to Fortune, the first programme began in Forest City in 2024. Participants reportedly paid about $1,500 a month, with accommodation, food, classes and access to facilities included.Why Forest City attracted technology workersForest City itself was hardly the main attraction for everyone who arrived. The appeal was the possibility of spending months around other people working on technology businesses, investing, engineering or internet-based projects. Instead of travelling between conferences and temporary coworking spaces, residents could live in one place with a ready-made professional network around them.The development had modern buildings and leisure facilities, while its location in Johor put Singapore within relatively easy reach. The surroundings were very different from the crowded technology centres usually associated with startups.For someone working remotely, a half-empty city could be useful. Residents described a routine built around shared meals, exercise, work and classes. The programme also attracted people interested in Srinivasan's broader ideas about technology, community and governance. Reports have described participants arriving from different countries, including digital nomads and young technology workers looking for a concentrated environment in which to build projects.Life inside the Network SchoolSome residents complained about mold in accommodation, something Srinivasan attributed in part to the humid local climate. Others found that Forest City lacked the restaurants, nightlife and variety of activities they might have expected from a major city. There were also complaints about the imbalance between men and women among participants.A group can work well online while remaining relatively loose. Living together exposes different problems. People have to share physical spaces, deal with maintenance and rules, and decide what happens when the surrounding town does not provide everything they want.The Network School could provide its own meals, activities and social environment. It could not easily manufacture an entire city around itself.What made Forest City such an unusual testStarting a new community usually requires expensive property, infrastructure and a large amount of planning. Network School did not have to build a city from scratch. It arrived at a place where towers, roads, hotels and amenities had already been constructed.The problem Forest City was facing was almost the reverse. That gave Srinivasan an unusually large experiment space. A community of technology workers could occupy part of an underused development without having to solve the enormous construction costs normally involved in establishing a new urban district.The arrangement also made the project's ambitions easier to observe. The Network School was not an abstract online community. People actually lived together, worked together and tried to form relationships around a shared set of ideas.Inside Forest City’s short-lived tech communityNetwork School remained tiny compared with the scale of Forest City. The development had been conceived for a population in the hundreds of thousands, while the school was dealing with hundreds of participants at most. Its presence therefore did not transform Forest City into a functioning metropolis.For a period, an otherwise underpopulated collection of towers became a meeting point for people interested in startups, cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence, digital communities and alternative forms of organisation. It offered something that conventional technology campuses generally cannot: the chance to live with the professional network rather than commute to it.A community can be highly active internally while remaining almost completely disconnected from the life around it. The Network School had its own routines and culture, but Forest City still had to operate according to Malaysian regulations and the commercial realities of the wider development.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: S Korea's revised espionage law: How it affects countries beyond North Korea
articles.summary: Rest of World News: South Korea implemented its expanded espionage law on Sunday, broadening espionage offences beyond acts involving North Korea to include all foreign c.
articles.body: South Korea implemented its expanded espionage law on Sunday, broadening espionage offences beyond acts involving North Korea to include all foreign countries.South Korea’s National Assembly had passed the revised Criminal Act on February 26. The amendment was promulgated on March 12 and comes into effect on Sunday, after a six-month grace period.The move comes after years of criticism that Seoul’s existing laws were ill-suited to punish technology and industrial espionage involving non-North Korean actors, especially China.The revised act carries a minimum sentence of three years in prison for the offence of conducting espionage for a foreign country or equivalent organisation. Existing provisions for espionage benefiting an “enemy state” remain in place.Earlier, prosecutors had to rely on other industrial technology or trade-secret laws, in many cases involving foreign entities.According to Reuters, Seoul’s national intelligence service welcomed the amendment when it was passed, saying it would strengthen South Korea’s ability to prevent leaks of strategic technologies such as semiconductors, displays, batteries and AI.Chinese espionage attemptsThe change follows high-profile technology leak cases, including last year’s indictment of five former Samsung Electronics employees accused of transferring key dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chip technology to Chinese memory maker CXMT.Asked whether the law, which does not specify any country, could be seen as targeting Beijing, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said China requires its enterprises to conduct international cooperation in accordance with international rules and laws.“At the same time, to this end, we believe that all countries should safeguard the normal investment and business activities of enterprises and provide a fair, just, and non-discriminatory business environment,” Mao told a regular news briefing on Friday.Earlier, the United States accused Chinese artificial intelligence firms, including DeepSeek and Alibaba, of stealing trade secrets from their American counterparts to cut development costs and swiftly release coveted technologies to the market.According to a joint advisory by USA’s Federal Bureau of Investigation, National Security Agency and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, major Chinese technology firms were found to be extracting “restricted proprietary functionalities and capabilities of US frontier AI models”, using “distillation” techniques, where smaller models are trained on more advanced architectures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ganesh Chaturthi 2026: What to do and what not to do after 'Ganpati Sthapana' and Ganesha's arrival at home
articles.summary: Trending News: There is a certain feeling when Ganpati comes home.The house may be full of people, there may be flowers everywhere, someone is busy making modaks whi.
articles.body: There is a certain feeling when Ganpati comes home.The house may be full of people, there may be flowers everywhere, someone is busy making modaks while another person is still trying to fix the decorations. And then comes the moment everyone has been waiting for - Ganpati Sthapana.Once Lord Ganesha is placed in the home, the celebrations begin. But for families that follow the traditional rituals, there are also a few things to keep in mind during the days Ganpati stays at home.These customs aren't exactly the same in every household. Some families follow elaborate puja rituals, while others keep things simple. The number of days the idol stays at home can also vary.Still, there are some common practices devotees usually follow after Ganpati Sthapana.Keep the space around Ganpati cleanThis is perhaps one of the simplest things to follow.Once the idol has been installed, the area around it should be kept clean. Flowers that have wilted, leftover food, used puja items and other waste shouldn't be allowed to pile up around the idol.And because the puja area tends to become a busy spot during Ganesh Chaturthi, it can get messy rather quickly. A little regular cleaning can make a big difference.Make time for daily pujaGanpati doesn't just arrive for the Sthapana and then become part of the home decor.Traditionally, devotees offer prayers every day while the idol is kept at home. Depending on the family's customs, this could include aarti, flowers, durva, sweets, fruits and other offerings.It doesn't have to be a lengthy ritual every single time. For some families, morning or evening aarti is enough. Others may have a more detailed puja routine.The important thing is to follow the tradition your family normally observes.Don't forget the modaksCan Ganesh Chaturthi really feel complete without modaks?The sweet is closely associated with Lord Ganesha and is commonly offered as prasad during the festival. Homemade modaks are a favourite in many homes, although ladoos, fruits and other vegetarian foods may also be offered.Once the offering has been made, the prasad can be shared with family members and guests.There is no need to turn every day's offering into a huge feast. A simple, fresh offering works perfectly well for families that prefer keeping the celebrations low-key.Be careful with food offeringsFresh food is generally preferred for puja.In Delhi's September heat, for example, milk-based sweets or other perishable foods shouldn't be left sitting outside for hours. Once the puja is over, food that needs refrigeration should be stored properly.And if something has spoiled, don't eat it simply because it was offered during the puja. Prasad should still be safe to consume.Try to keep the atmosphere peacefulGanesh Chaturthi can get loud and lively, especially when relatives and friends start dropping in for darshan.That's part of the fun.But traditionally, the period is also seen as a time for prayer and devotion. So unnecessary arguments, fights or deliberately disruptive behaviour around the puja area are best avoided.Nobody expects a household to suddenly become completely silent for 10 days. Families will talk, children will play and guests will come over. The idea is simply to maintain a respectful atmosphere around Ganpati.Don't move the idol unnecessarilyOnce the Sthapana has been performed, devotees generally avoid moving the idol without a reason.The exact customs can differ, particularly depending on how and where the idol has been installed. So if there is a genuine need to shift it, families may prefer to follow the guidance of their priest or the tradition they have been following for years.This is one area where there isn't necessarily one rule that applies to every home.Follow your family's tradition for VisarjanOne of the biggest questions around Ganpati is often: When should the visarjan happen?There isn't one answer for every household.Some families bring Ganpati home for one and a half days. Others keep the idol for three, five, seven or 10 days. Some families follow different timings altogether.The visarjan day is usually decided according to the family's tradition and, in some cases, the preferred muhurat.So if your neighbour is doing visarjan on a different day, there's no reason to assume your family is doing something wrong.Don't turn the festival into a wasteful celebrationWith flowers, decorations, food and guests, it is easy for the amount of waste at home to go up during Ganesh Chaturthi.There are simple ways around that.Reusable decorations can be used instead of buying new ones every year. Food can be prepared according to the number of people actually expected at home. And flowers and other puja waste can be disposed of responsibly.Many families also choose eco-friendly Ganpati idols, particularly because of concerns around the impact of immersion on water bodies.What about non-vegetarian food?This is another area where customs can differ.Many families follow a vegetarian diet during the period Ganpati is at home, while others may have their own established practices. Some households avoid certain foods only on the main puja days.There is no need to assume that every family follows exactly the same food rules. If your household has a particular tradition, that's the one to follow.Don't get too stressed about getting every ritual perfectThis may be the most useful thing to remember.Ganesh Chaturthi comes with plenty of rituals, and if you're celebrating at home for the first time, it can sometimes feel like there is a long list of things you're supposed to remember.But traditions aren't identical across India. A Maharashtrian household may have different customs from a family in Delhi, Gujarat, Karnataka or Bengal. Even two families from the same city may celebrate differently.If you're unsure about a particular ritual, check with your family priest or an elder who knows your family's tradition rather than relying on random rules circulating online.At its heart, Ganesh Chaturthi is about welcoming Lord Ganesha into the home with devotion and joy.So keep the puja space clean, offer fresh food and prayers, treat the idol with respect and follow the customs your family believes in.And yes, make those modaks. Ganpati would probably expect nothing less.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: A Tanzanian biologist fed bacteria discarded fruit and vegetables to replace fishmeal; the resulting feed reportedly brought fish to market 40% sooner and raised farmers’ profits 25%
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Diana Orembe, a Tanzanian biologist, is transforming fish farming by creating sustainable feed from discarded fruits and vegetables, resulting in faster growth and increased profits for farmers.
articles.body: In much of East Africa, small-scale fish farming seems easy enough on paper, but it keeps hitting the same wall: the cost of feeding the fish. In Tanzania, feed alone can account for around seventy percent of the expenditures of running a small farm, and much of that feed relies on either imported soybean or fishmeal manufactured from wild-caught fish, both of which come with hefty price tags and environmental impacts of their own. But for Diana Orembe, a biologist working in Dar es Salaam, the imbalance seemed less like an inevitable aspect of the industry and more like a problem waiting for the proper kind of microbe.Orembe co-founded the biotech firm NovFeed before being selected by UNICEF Innovation as one of its young innovators addressing climate-related challenges. The basic material is leftover fruit and vegetables collected from schools, universities and local markets across the city, garbage that would otherwise simply rot. UNICEF Innovation included Orembe in its cohort of young innovators addressing climate-related challenges. Her company, NovFeed, uses bacterial fermentation to convert discarded vegetables into a protein ingredient for fish feed.Making fish food out of garbageThe procedure involves adding a special blend of bacteria to the collected waste, and the microbes consume the material, reassembling its nutrients into a concentrated protein for farmed fish. Dar es Salaam produces thousands of tonnes of waste every day, a lot of it organic; thus, the raw material for this process is almost endless and almost free, an entirely different starting point than buying soybean meal from the other side of the planet. The resulting feed also floats instead of sinking, which can reduce feed losses when conventional pellets settle on the pond floor before fish consume them.NovFeed’s process starts with organic waste collected mainly from schools, universities and markets in Dar es Salaam. The company separates useful organic material before fermentation, allowing its microbes to act as a biological factory that converts the waste into single-cell protein for fish feed. UNICEF says the main ingredients are agri-waste and bacterial cells, and that the resulting protein can replace traditional fishmeal and soybean. The process also avoids dependence on wild-caught fish as a protein source and turns organic waste into an input for aquaculture rather than leaving it to decompose. NovFeed was established in 2020, and the company has continued developing the technology with an emphasis on scaling the protein for fish-feed production.More growth, more profitsThe actual outcomes have been measured directly on farms and not merely in a laboratory. Fish that were fed the fermented feed reached market weight about forty per cent faster than fish fed conventional feed, and farmers that used the fermented feed reported a twenty-five per cent increase in their total profits. The approach also reduces reliance on fishmeal made from wild-caught fish, easing pressure on marine fish stocks that would otherwise be used as feed.Recognition beyond the farm gateThe wider food and sustainability world has taken notice too. The project was later highlighted by the Food Planet Prize, while NovFeed went on to win a $1-million Milken-Motsepe Prize in AgriTech. What began as a solution to a single country’s feed issue has become a demonstration of something larger: that the garbage sitting in a market bin may be worth more to a fish farmer than the imported alternatives propping up the sector. The bacteria did the heavy job, but it needed a biologist prepared to see decaying fruit as an opportunity, not an issue, to make the notion work.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2015, UNICEF turned shipping containers into heated bathrooms for Mongolia’s nomadic schools; 15 movable WASH Houses gave warm water and toilets to 1,400 students
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how UNICEF's WASH Houses are revolutionizing sanitation and hygiene for nomadic schoolchildren in Mongolia, providing heated toilets and warm water to ensure their well-being even in extreme winter conditions.
articles.body: For children in Mongolia’s remote herding communities, using a toilet could mean leaving a heated classroom and stepping outside into temperatures far below freezing. Many rural schools and kindergartens depended on outdoor latrines, while access to warm water for washing was limited. The problem was especially difficult in a country where nomadic families move with their livestock and frozen ground can complicate conventional construction.According to UNICEF, the organisation developed relocatable WASH Houses in Mongolia by adapting the principles of insulated shipping-container construction. The units provided toilets and basins with warm running water in heated, well-lit structures that could be connected to classrooms or ger kindergartens. By 2015, 15 WASH Houses had been installed alongside ger kindergartens and regular classrooms, directly benefiting about 1,400 students.Building a bathroom that could survive winterThe WASH House was developed as a prefabricated and relocatable solution for Mongolia's harsh climate. The organisation worked with local partners to develop several models based on insulated shipping-container structures. Rather than building every facility from scratch at the school site, the units could be manufactured elsewhere and transported to remote communities. The design addressed one of the biggest problems facing sanitation infrastructure in Mongolia: freezing temperatures. The units were insulated and heated, while their water and sanitation systems were designed to operate in winter conditions. They contained toilets and washing facilities supplied with warm water, giving children access to basic hygiene without having to leave the building for an outdoor latrine.The facility’s portability was especially useful for ger schools and kindergartens. A ger is a round tent-like home traditionally used by Mongolian herding families, and schools in remote areas often have to adapt to that way of life. A portable sanitation facility can offer more flexibility compared to a regular building made of bricks and concrete. UNICEF said the units could be adapted to different water and sanitation setups depending on the site. Some could use wells and septic tanks, while others could connect to existing systems.Warm water became part of school lifeIt was not just about making toilets available to them. Water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities affect whether students can access washrooms, maintain personal hygiene, and use toilets safely during the day. UNICEF research on WASH and menstrual health also noted that rural students in Mongolia faced special challenges because sanitation facilities were inadequate and water and separate washing rooms were limited.Research published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health also examined hygiene conditions among Mongolian schoolchildren. A survey of 1,507 fifth-grade pupils in Ulaanbaatar found that access to water and soap at school handwashing facilities was far from universal, showing how infrastructure availability can shape everyday hygiene practices. For the children using the new WASH Houses, the difference was tangible. UNICEF described facilities that allowed pupils to wash with warm water and use toilets inside a heated structure instead of relying on exposed outdoor facilities. The organisation reported that the teachers linked the better WASH conditions with the lack of health-related issues and absenteeism, but this information was not a part of the scientifically controlled evaluation of the WASH Houses. These units solved multiple problems by improving sanitation, reducing children’s exposure to extreme winter weather, and making handwashing easier.A shipping container becomes school infrastructureThe project reflected a broader trend toward designing infrastructure for places where conventional construction is costly or impractical. Mongolia has a short construction season, harsh winters, and long distances between settlements. As a result, it can be difficult to transport materials and build facilities in remote locations. A prefabricated container offered another option, since much of the work could be completed before delivery and the facility could then be connected to local water and sanitation services.The approach did not aim to turn shipping containers into an alternative to regular schools but rather showed that the infrastructure could be adapted to suit the location. An insulated, heated, and mobile bathroom could be built where it was needed without erecting a whole new permanent structure. In remote Mongolian schools, it became a way to provide toilets, hot water, and basic hygiene facilities for children who previously had to endure harsh conditions to meet basic needs.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1973, Ontario teacher Hank Deverell built his wife a bottle house for her doll collection; about 25,000 glass bottles and 1,750 hours later, it became a roadside attraction
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 1973, Ontario teacher Hank Deverell and his wife Myrtle built a house from glass bottles in Redditt, a small community in northwestern Ontario, Can.
articles.body: In 1973, Ontario teacher Hank Deverell and his wife Myrtle built a house from glass bottles in Redditt, a small community in northwestern Ontario, Canada. Myrtle wanted a house to display her growing doll collection, and Hank turned the idea into a bottle-built structure that later became a local tourist attraction.The Redditt Bottle House is located along Highway 658, about 20 minutes north of Kenora. The property was created in the early 1970s and includes the bottle house along with other glass and fantasy-themed structures. The unusual construction has since drawn visitors to the area.According to the Kenora Great War Project, Myrtle was previously married to Orley Edgar Neuert, a former Canadian soldier who served with the 13th Battalion during the First World War. Orley and Myrtle had four children and later lived in Redditt, where Orley worked for the Canadian National Railway as a storekeeper and baggageman.Orley died in 1964. Myrtle later married Hank Deverell, who worked as a teacher at Beaver Brae High School in Kenora. The couple lived in Redditt, and in 1973 they built the bottle house to give Myrtle a place to display her doll collection.The structure was made using thousands of glass bottles held together with mortar. About 25,000 bottles and 1,000 pounds of mortar were used to build the attraction. The Deverells also spent about 1,750 hours on the construction.The bottles became the main feature of the property. Village Life described the house as a structure that uses glass to create patterns of colour and light.The property was not limited to the main house. It also came to include a glass windmill and a structure known as the “House of the Three Bears”. These were designed in the same fantasy style as the bottle house.The bottle house did not remain only a personal project for Myrtle and Hank. It soon began attracting visitors. Village Life reported that about 1,500 people visited when the Bottle House first opened in the summer of 1973. Visitors have since travelled from different parts of Canada and other countries to see the glass structures. The attraction also became part of Redditt’s local identity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 10 countries with the highest forest cover in the world; check India’s rank
articles.summary: For travellers who love greens and dream of disappearing into dense rainforests, walking beneath towering trees or spotting wildlife far from crowded .
articles.body: For travellers who love greens and dream of disappearing into dense rainforests, walking beneath towering trees or spotting wildlife far from crowded tourist trails, some countries offer a very different kind of holiday experience. The Worldometer ranking, based on FAOSTAT data, puts Russia, Brazil, Canada, the United States, China, DR Congo, Australia, Indonesia, Peru and India among the top 10 countries by total forest area.Let’s take a deeper look at these countries forest side:Russia (814.8 million hectares)Russia has by far the world's largest forest area, with 814,848,460 hectares of forest. Much of this forest belt forms part of the taiga, the vast boreal forest stretching across Siberia. It is a landscape of conifers, lakes, rivers and long winters. These forests are also natural home to wildlife including brown bears, wolves, lynx and the Siberian tiger. For travellers, Russia's forests offer experiences ranging from remote Siberian wilderness to the forests surrounding Lake Baikal.Brazil (491.57 million hectares)Brazil comes second with 491,570,000 hectares of forest. The country's forest story is dominated by the Amazon, the world's largest tropical rainforest. Travellers visiting Brazil can experience the rainforest around destinations such as Manaus, where river journeys offer access to the Amazon's extraordinary ecosystem.Canada (346.98 million hectares)The third spot is taken by Canada with 346,975,800 hectares of forest. Its forests stretch across huge parts of the country, creating some of the world's most dramatic wilderness landscapes. For travellers, Canada's forests are closely connected with hiking, camping, canoeing and wildlife watching. Bears, moose, wolves and other wildlife can be encountered across different regions.United States (310.65 million hectares)The United States has 310,645,000 hectares of forest, making it the fourth-largest country by total forest area. Travellers can explore the giant trees of California and the Pacific Northwest to the Appalachian forests in the east and the boreal landscapes of Alaska.China (211.41 million hectares)China ranks fifth with 211,405,700 hectares of forest. The country's forests range from subtropical landscapes in the south to temperate and mountainous forests farther north.The bamboo forests around Chengdu and Sichuan offer encounters with giant pandas, while mountainous forest landscapes can be found around destinations such as Zhangjiajie.Democratic Republic of the Congo (151.96 million hectares)The sixth spot is taken by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). It has 151,955,200 hectares of forest. Much of this forest forms part of the Congo Basin, one of the world's most important tropical rainforest regions. For adventurous travellers, the country's forests offer rare wildlife experiences. The DRC is home to mountain gorillas, eastern lowland gorillas, chimpanzees and the endangered bonobo.Australia (125.37 million hectares)Australia ranks seventh on the list with 125,367,000 hectares of forest. Its forests look very different and are eucalyptus dominated. Travellers can explore forests around Queensland's Daintree Rainforest, one of Australia's best-known tropical forest destinations, or experience the country's vast eucalyptus landscapes.Indonesia (89.64 million hectares)Indonesia ranks eighth with 89,641,200 hectares of forest. For travellers, some of the most memorable forest experiences can be found on islands such as Sumatra, Borneo and Papua. Sumatra's forests, for instance, are among the places where visitors can seek out orangutans in their natural habitat.Peru (73.64 million hectares)Peru is on the ninth spot on the list with 73,637,800 hectares of forest globally. While Peru is internationally famous for Machu Picchu and the Andes, a huge part of its natural landscape lies in the Amazon Basin. Destinations such as Tambopata and the Amazon around Iquitos offer travellers a very different side of Peru.India (71.04 million hectares)India rounds off the top 10 with 71,038,800 hectares of forest. Travellers can find Himalayan forests in the north, tropical forests in the Western Ghats and Northeast, dry deciduous forests across central India and mangrove ecosystems along the coast. Some of the country's most popular wildlife destinations are forest-based, including Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Corbett, Kaziranga and Ranthambore.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Iran-linked groups used Claude to target US Navy, run propaganda: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iranian state-aligned and Iran-linked groups used Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence platform to run propaganda campaigns, conduct domestic su.
articles.body: Iranian state-aligned and Iran-linked groups used Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence platform to run propaganda campaigns, conduct domestic surveillance and develop targeting recommendations against US naval forces, according to a threat report released by the company.Anthropic said it disrupted malicious activity involving Claude between December 2025 and August 2026, covering cyber operations, influence campaigns and surveillance. The company said several Iranian-linked accounts had used the AI model to automate or support activities ranging from producing state propaganda to analysing social media users and gathering information on US military positions.The findings come amid heightened tensions between Iran and the United States, including attacks involving US and Iranian forces around the Strait of Hormuz. Commercial shipping through the waterway has remained limited as the conflict has continued, with Iran seeking greater control over traffic passing through the strategic strait.Claude used to build Iranian propaganda campaignsAnthropic said it identified and removed three accounts aligned with Iranian state propaganda institutions. The accounts were linked to the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization under Iran’s Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, the Islamic Propaganda Office of Khorasan Razavi and the Islamic Propaganda Organization’s Bina Cultural Observatory.According to Anthropic, the accounts used Claude to develop campaign plans, propaganda doctrine manuals, personas and target databases. They also converted official government intelligence bulletins into tailored content in Farsi, Arabic, Urdu, Malay, Spanish and English, with plans for distribution in as many as 20 languages.The material was spread across X, Instagram, Telegram, TikTok and YouTube, as well as Iranian platforms including Eitaa, Bale and Rubika. Anthropic said some of the content appeared on channels sympathetic to Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) narratives.The company assessed the influence operation as Category Three on its Breakout Scale, indicating that the activity involved distribution across multiple platforms.During the 2026 US-Israel-Iran war, Anthropic said the network also attributed false claims to Western research organisations, including CSIS, Brookings and RAND, in an apparent attempt to make Iranian state-backed narratives appear more credible.Iran-linked account developed US naval targeting toolsAnthropic separately identified an Iran-linked account that used Claude to collect and analyse publicly available information about US naval forces in the region.The account used the AI model to compile targeting handbooks and identify and track naval positions using open-source information, according to the company. Anthropic said the activity involved developing recommendations that could potentially be used against US naval forces.The threat report also detailed the use of Claude by Iranian paramilitary and security-linked units for domestic surveillance. Anthropic said it banned 16 accounts operated by two linked units associated with Iranian paramilitary and security agencies.One organisation claimed to have surveilled and profiled 6,388 Iranians in a single year and maintained an identity database. Anthropic said Claude was used to help build what it assessed was likely a government-controlled surveillance case-management system and to analyse 155,216 tweets.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Might makes right’ logic should have been discarded long ago: Xi at Brics Summit
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Chinese president Xi Jinping on Sunday called on Global South countries to jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs and stre.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chinese president Xi Jinping on Sunday called on Global South countries to jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs and strengthen cooperation across areas including artificial intelligence, trade, digital industries, manufacturing and science and technology.His remarks came at the second session of the 18th Brics Summit, where he also said China would continue opening its economy and sharing the opportunities of its development with other countries.Addressing the summit, Xi said international rules must be written by all countries and rejected the logic of “might makes right”. He called for the principles of sovereign equality, noninterference in internal affairs and peaceful settlement of disputes to be upheld, with international law and rules applied to all without double standards."Fairness and justice is a universal aspiration, and international rules must be written by all countries. The logic of “might makes right” does not hold, and should have been discarded long ago. Global South countries should jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs, safeguard the basic norms of international relations including sovereign equality, noninterference in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and ensure that international law and international rules are applied to all, free from double standards," Xi said.Xi also urged Global South countries to remain committed to a people-centred development philosophy and work towards the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. He said that since China launched the Global Development Initiative five years ago, it had implemented more than 2,000 projects in partnership with other countries and provided training to more than 200,000 professionals, benefiting people in more than 120 countries.He added China had granted zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations and would continue to broaden independent and unilateral opening up."China is opening its door ever wider to the world. We have granted zero-tariff treatment for all the 53 African countries having diplomatic relations with China. We will continue to broaden independent and unilateral opening up, and share the opportunities of China’s development with other countries," the Chinese president said.Five initiatives for Brics cooperationXi proposed five initiatives to strengthen BRICS cooperation, focusing on artificial intelligence, trade and investment, digital industries, intelligent manufacturing, and science and technology talent development.Under the open source and inclusive AI initiative, China will work to establish a Brics AI open source community, support cooperation in developing and applying large language models, organise specialised AI seminars and training courses, and build an open AI ecosystem.On trade and investment facilitation, Xi proposed a BRICS special economic zone partnership through which countries could establish an intelligent portal, coordinate policies and build a new frontier for open development. He also said China would host the BRICS Forum on Trade in Services next year.The digital industry cooperation initiative envisages a Brics digital ecosystem cloud platform, along with digital skills training, technological exchanges and industrial alignment.Under the intelligent manufacturing initiative, China offered to assist fellow Brics countries in building smart factories and developing standards and norms to promote manufacturing transformation and upgrading.Xi also proposed a Brics engineer cultivation alliance for the joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards. China will launch a Brics youth exchange programme focused on scientific and technological innovation.‘Greater Brics’ push gains momentumXi also unveiled initiatives spanning areas from AI to trade to deepen cooperation among the “Greater Brics” emerging economies, as Beijing seeks to strengthen the grouping as a practical platform for Global South development.Political and security cooperation, along with economic and financial cooperation, remain the grouping’s main focus areas, with India as the 2026 chair and China set to take over in 2027 as the two countries seek wider partnerships to boost Brics’ global clout.The success of the "Greater Brics Initiative" depends on laying a solid foundation for pragmatic cooperation, Xi told the leaders' ​annual summit in New Delhi, the official Xinhua news agency said.'Greater Brics' nations should further co-operate, maintain ⁠the stability of industrial and supply chains, and cultivate an integrated market, Xi told the summit's closing session, as cited by Reuters.Brics has expanded from its original membership of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa to include Iran, Indonesia, Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates.It also has 10 partner countries spanning emerging economies across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East, further broadening its reach across the Global South.China and Russia sometimes refer to the expanded bloc as "Greater Brics".PM Modi-Xi meeting focuses on ties and border peaceOn the sidelines of the summit, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Xi held a 40-minute meeting during which they agreed that India and China should take a strategic and long-term view of their relationship and ensure that differences do not turn into disputes.Xi said the current momentum in bilateral ties, built on the resumption of institutional exchanges, an expanding cooperation agenda and growing trade, had been hard-won and should be cherished.PM Modi welcomed the “steady progress” in bilateral relations but underlined that peace and tranquillity in the border areas would remain an essential basis for the continued development of ties.The meeting was the leaders’ third bilateral interaction in two years, following their meetings in Kazan in 2024 and Tianjin last year. It was also their first meeting on Indian soil in seven years.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: China’s new anti-drone weapon is laser on wheels: Why it matters for modern warfare
articles.summary: International News: China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) appears to be developing an amphibious armoured vehicle fitted with a laser weapon and additional sensors to co.
articles.body: China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) appears to be developing an amphibious armoured vehicle fitted with a laser weapon and additional sensors to counter drones, potentially giving frontline forces greater protection during a possible Taiwan landing operation. The new variant of the Type 19 8x8 combat vehicle was seen in unverified images posted on Chinese social media on August 29, as Taiwan moves to rapidly expand its own drone capabilities.The development comes as Taipei prepares to spend billions of dollars on uncrewed systems. On September 3, Taiwan’s cabinet proposed a NT$145.7 billion ($4.6 billion) supplementary defence budget that includes more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones and over 40,000 coastal attack drones. The package still needs legislative approval.The combination points to a battlefield in which drones could play a major role on both sides. For PLA forces attempting to land and establish a foothold in Taiwan, a mobile system capable of detecting and disabling drones could help protect troops and armoured vehicles from attacks and surveillance.The Type 19 family is already associated with PLA amphibious formations. Defence intelligence provider Janes reported in 2023 that vehicles from the family had entered service with the 73rd Group Army under the Eastern Theatre Command. The command includes amphibious brigades that would be expected to play a major role in any Taiwan landing operation.If the newly seen vehicle retains the Type 19's amphibious capability, it could potentially accompany troops during an assault and provide short-range protection against uncrewed surveillance aircraft and loitering munitions.Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum and a former senior China analyst at Rand Corporation and for the US military, said it was difficult to know without more technical data whether the modifications affected the Type 19’s amphibious performance, but he believed operating the laser system while afloat “should be possible”.The vehicle's additional equipment could, however, create technical challenges. The laser, sensors and associated systems would add weight to an amphibious platform where buoyancy is critical. The equipment would also have to withstand exposure to salt water.Heath said the added weight could potentially be offset by reducing the crew size or other equipment, although the system would also need to be protected from salt water.Taiwan is building a large drone forceTaiwan has been expanding its use of uncrewed systems as it prepares for a potential conflict with China. Days before the proposed supplementary budget, Taiwanese lawmakers approved a separate six-year NT$240 billion framework for domestically produced drones after rejecting a competing government plan.The island has also reorganised parts of its military around drone warfare.The army finalised drone battalions across three operational combat zones in April. The marine corps had earlier established a drone battalion as part of a restructuring that also included disbanding tank and self-propelled artillery battalions.During Taiwan's Han Kuang 42 military exercise in August, aerial drone units carried out battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance, intelligence transmission and attack missions, according to the island's defence ministry.For an amphibious force, drones could pose several threats beyond direct attacks. They could track troop movements, identify vehicles and positions and help direct artillery, missiles and other weapons towards exposed forces.That makes a mobile counter-drone system potentially valuable during the most vulnerable phase of a landing operation.Heath said the laser-based counter-drone system could be “very useful in a Taiwan conflict” in which Taiwanese forces might use drone swarms to target amphibious vehicles coming ashore.The cost of firing a laser can also be much lower than repeatedly using conventional missiles or ammunition against relatively inexpensive drones. That could become important in a conflict involving large numbers of uncrewed systems.Heath added that the laser system’s low operating cost could make it particularly useful against such attacks.Lessons from Ukraine and earlier drone warfareThe apparent development also fits a wider shift in military thinking after recent conflicts demonstrated how vulnerable armoured and frontline forces can be to drones.In the Russia-Ukraine war, uncrewed aircraft have been used extensively for reconnaissance, artillery spotting and attacks on tanks, artillery and other military equipment.Heath said the new Type 19 variant was consistent with lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war, where drones had proved effective against tanks, artillery and other frontline targets, increasing the value of mounting counter-drone systems directly on individual platforms.He said the PLA had “almost certainly” drawn similar lessons from earlier fighting between Armenia and Azerbaijan, where drones had shown an ability to bypass traditional air-defence systems.Those lessons appear to be driving a broader PLA effort to protect troops and vehicles from drones. Possible approaches include additional armour, conventional guns and missiles, as well as newer directed-energy systems such as lasers and microwave weapons.The Type 19 could represent another step in that evolution by putting sensors and counter-drone capabilities directly on an armoured vehicle that can move with mechanised formations.Other militaries are pursuing similar concepts.South Korea's Hanwha this week unveiled a Tigon 8x8 armoured vehicle fitted with a 50-kilowatt counter-drone laser. The company has built a prototype and plans serial production by the end of 2027.In the United States, AeroVironment's 20kW-class Locust system has been mounted on Army Joint Light Tactical Vehicles. JLTV-mounted Locust systems were delivered to the US Army in December under a prototyping programme.The PLA system seen in the Type 19 images, however, remains less certain.Janes assessed the vehicle as a Type 19-based counter-drone variant, but it is not clear whether it is operational, undergoing trials or being used only as a technology demonstrator.Why the laser matters, and its limitsA laser could give an amphibious formation a potentially deep magazine against drones because it does not rely on carrying a conventional interceptor for every target. It could also complement existing guns and other air-defence weapons.But directed-energy weapons have limitations.Their effectiveness can be reduced by weather, smoke and dust. They also require substantial electrical power and cooling. These factors could be particularly important during a contested amphibious operation, where vehicles may have limited opportunities for maintenance or resupply.That may explain why the newly seen vehicle appears to retain its autocannon alongside the laser and additional sensors.The combination would give crews more than one way to respond to a drone threat. A laser could be used when conditions allow, while the cannon could provide another option against targets that are difficult to engage with directed energy.The larger significance of the Type 19 variant may therefore lie less in the laser itself and more in how the PLA appears to be adapting armoured forces for a battlefield increasingly shaped by drones.If the vehicle eventually enters operational service, it could provide amphibious units with a mobile layer of counter-drone protection as they move towards and across Taiwan's coastline. But until more information emerges about its performance, power requirements, amphibious capability and operational status, its role in a future conflict remains uncertain.

articles.title: In 2001, a Houston baby needed a liver transplant as US flights were grounded; strangers moved the organ 800 miles by C-130, and 25 years later she is in law school
articles.summary: US News: On September 11, 2001, while the US was dealing with the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, a six-month-old baby in Houston was fighting for her.
articles.body: On September 11, 2001, while the US was dealing with the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, a six-month-old baby in Houston was fighting for her life. Kareena needed a liver transplant, but the donor organ was nearly 800 miles away in Nashville, and the civilian flights across the US had been grounded.The liver, packed in ice inside a box roughly two feet by one foot, eventually reached Houston aboard a C-130 cargo plane, Houston Chronicle reported. The aircraft, operated by the Tennessee Air National Guard, carried the organ from Nashville to Ellington Field. From there, soldiers took it to Texas Children’s Hospital, where doctors were waiting to perform the transplant.Kareena had been born with biliary atresia, a congenital defect in which the ducts that drain bile from the liver do not form. Because the bile could not drain properly, her liver became badly damaged at a very young age. By September 2001, she had spent most of her short life in the Texas Medical Center and was too sick to go home.“She was too ill to leave the hospital,” Dr John Goss, the hospital’s medical director for transplant services, told Houstone Chronicle, 25 years after the transplant. “She was very sick, and she wasn’t going to survive very long without a transplant,” he added.The chance of a transplant came on the night of September 10, when Goss received a call from his former colleague at Vanderbilt University, Dr Ravi Chari. A liver that could match the six-month-old’s size and blood type was available in Nashville.Transplant disrupted by 9/11The original plan was Chari would remove the liver in Nashville, Tennessee Donor Services would arrange a charter flight to Houston, and Goss would transplant the organ into Kareena.That plan changed the next morning. Goss was treating adult patients at St Luke’s when the first plane hit the World Trade Center in New York. He later recalled, “It’s weird. I can still remember we were in a patient room when the first jet flew into the tower.”A second plane hit the World Trade Center soon after. As the attacks unfolded in New York, Washington, DC, and Pennsylvania, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every civilian aircraft in the country.In Nashville, Chari was still in the operating room with the donor liver. The charter flight that was supposed to carry the organ was no longer possible.Jill Grandas, who was then a coordinator with Tennessee Donor Services and is now its CEO, was told that the flight had been cancelled. A road journey to Houston was considered but rejected. At the time, the organ could not survive the roughly 12-hour drive.Grandas then went to the mail room, took out a phone book and called the air-traffic control tower at Nashville International Airport. She explained that a baby in Houston would die without the liver waiting in the operating room.The supervisor who answered understood the situation. Grandas later learnt that the woman had a relative on a transplant waiting list.Within minutes, another option emerged. The Tennessee Air National Guard agreed to fly the liver to Houston. “It was a feeling of joy in the midst of something so tragic,” Grandas said. “We were determined that we weren’t going to let another person die as a result of that attack.”Military plane carried the tiny liverNine National Guard members boarded a C-130 Hercules aircraft and flew the liver to Houston. The aircraft can carry up to 47,000 pounds, but on that flight its important cargo was a liver small enough to fit inside a box packed with ice.The plane landed at Ellington Field within a few hours. At noon, the organ was handed over to another group of soldiers. They drove it towards Texas Children’s Hospital in a military vehicle.The liver then reached Goss, who was waiting to perform the transplant. By that evening, Kareena had received the organ.“Even though there was the horrific event and it was meant to hurt a lot of people, there were still very good people who were not going to let it completely hurt us,” Goss said. “In the end, the good will win.”For Grandas, the successful journey of the organ was possible because everyone involved continued to find a way forward.“Nobody ever said no,” she said. “Not the staff at the hospital, not the FAA or the National Guard. We had a mission to get this liver to Houston. And we did.”Kareena remembers her savioursThe transplant gave Kareena the chance to grow up. Twenty-five years later, she is still living in the Houston area. She graduated from college and is now studying health policy in law school. She hopes to work in health equity. “I want to make the most of the life that so many strangers worked to give me,” she said.Kareena continues to remember the people who helped her survive. Every September 11, she calls Grandas in Nashville. The two met in person for the first time only recently, when Grandas travelled to Houston.On September 11, 2026, Kareena also returned to Texas Children’s Hospital, where Goss had performed the transplant 25 years earlier. The two have reunited several times since the surgery, although they had not met for a couple of years.Kareena greeted Goss with a hug and later took a selfie with him for her mother. But both said the story was bigger than their reunion.The liver had come from a Tennessee family that had lost an infant on the night of September 10, 2001. In the middle of that loss, the family chose to donate the infant’s organ so another child could live.“They didn’t just save a life,” Kareena said. “They created a family. They created friendships, communities,” she added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: From one glass of milk to a 35-year legacy: How one Bihar tea seller’s kindness to babies became a family mission that lives on
articles.summary: At a small tea stall near the Rajgir Bus Stand in Bihar’s Nalanda district, a simple sign carries a message that has quietly touched thousands of live.
articles.body: At a small tea stall near the Rajgir Bus Stand in Bihar’s Nalanda district, a simple sign carries a message that has quietly touched thousands of lives: children from birth to 18 months can get milk for free. What began as one tea seller’s response to a mother struggling to feed her baby has continued for more than three decades. The story began in 1990, when Shravan Kumar was running his tea shop in Rajgir. According to reports by Hindustan and ETV Bharat, he noticed that some families visiting the area struggled to arrange milk for their young children. Instead of simply feeling sorry for them, Shravan decided to do something himself. He began providing milk to infants without asking their families for payment.A small tea stall with a big promiseShravan’s decision was simple: if a baby needed milk, the family could come to his shop and get it without worrying about the cost. According to Hindustan, the tea stall eventually became known for providing free milk to children up to 18 months old. The service was not presented as a temporary campaign or a publicity exercise. It became part of the shop’s identity. A board outside the stall informed people that milk was available free of cost for babies from birth to 18 months. ETV Bharat’s report gives a more personal account of how the initiative began. It says Shravan once heard a baby crying near his shop and realised the child was hungry. He gave the mother a glass of milk for the baby. When the child stopped crying after drinking it, the experience stayed with him. He then decided to continue providing milk to young children who needed it.What makes the story especially striking is that Shravan reportedly did not want others to finance the initiative. Oneindia, which also reported on the tea stall, says people offered donations after learning about his work, but Shravan chose to continue the service himself. For him, helping a hungry child was not something that needed recognition.After Shravan’s death, his brother kept the promise aliveShravan died in 2000, but the service did not end with him. His younger brother, Ranjit Kumar, popularly known as Tunna Baba, took responsibility for the tea stall and continued the tradition started by his brother. Hindustan reported in November 2023 that Ranjit had been providing free milk to children for 33 years, counting the years since Shravan first started the initiative in 1990. The story is therefore not simply about one generous tea seller. It is also about a family choosing to preserve an act of kindness long after the person who started it was gone. According to Nalanda Live, Ranjit said he distributes around 3 to 4 litres of milk every day, while the requirement can rise to around 10 to 15 litres during busy periods such as the Malmas Mela, when Rajgir sees a large number of visitors. The report also said that the family finances the service through its own earnings rather than relying on outside donations.“What will I take with me?”Perhaps the most powerful part of Ranjit’s story is his attitude towards money. Speaking to Nalanda Live, Ranjit reportedly said that he spends part of the tea shop’s earnings on the milk and does not feel the need to accumulate everything for himself. The report quoted him expressing the belief that material wealth cannot be taken along after death, while the blessings of people can bring a different kind of satisfaction. That philosophy has turned an ordinary tea shop into an unexpected place of support for families. The stall is located near the Rajgir Bus Stand, an area frequented by local residents, travellers and tourists. People who notice the sign can approach the shop when their young children need milk. Hindustan reported that visitors have also praised Ranjit’s work and shared pictures and posts about the initiative on social media.A legacy built one glass at a timeThere are many stories of charity that begin with large donations, organisations or fundraising campaigns. Shravan Kumar’s story began with something much smaller: a glass of milk. He saw a problem in front of him and chose to respond with whatever he could offer. His contribution may have appeared modest, but repeating that small act every day turned it into a decades-long tradition. Today, the Shravan Tea Stall carries the name of the man who started the initiative, while Ranjit continues to keep his brother’s promise alive. The story is a reminder that social service does not always require wealth, influence or a large organisation.Sometimes, it begins when an ordinary person notices someone else’s need and decides not to look away. More than 30 years after Shravan first offered milk to a hungry child, his family continues to serve young children at the same tea stall in Rajgir. And perhaps that is the most meaningful part of the story: his kindness did not end with him. It became a tradition.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: 'Stepmotherly treatment': Tejashwi seeks 'national disaster' tag for Bihar floods, slams Centre's response
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Bihar leader of opposition Tejashwi Yadav on Sunday accused the PM Modi-led Centre of giving the state \"stepmotherly\" treatment in flood re.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bihar leader of opposition Tejashwi Yadav on Sunday accused the PM Modi-led Centre of giving the state "stepmotherly" treatment in flood relief, while seeking a "national disaster" tag for the flood situation.Addressing a press conference in Patna, the RJD working president criticised chief minister Samrat Choudhary and Union ministers from Bihar for "failing to secure a relief package for Bihar"."Whenever there are floods in Gujarat, Prime Minister Narendra Modi gives quick assurances of relief, talks to state leadership and directs deployment of relief forces, including the Indian Air Force. However, there is a step-motherly treatment towards Bihar where he comes during election campaigns and eats 'litti chokha'," Tejashwi alleged.Tejashwi said he wrote to PM Modi on September 7, seeking that the floods be declared a "national disaster" and demanding immediate financial assistance of Rs 5,000 crore."The engines of the 'double-engine' government in Bihar have failed. I am not aware of how often the CM talks to PM Modi, and wonder why he has not been able to secure central assistance. There are many Union ministers from Bihar, but none has the influence to bring central help to Bihar," he said.Tejashwi also claimed that he had received no response to letters he wrote to PM Modi and Choudhary."Just like PM has ignored Bihar in times of flood, people will ignore him in the future," he said.The water levels of rivers in north Bihar have risen amid massive flooding in Nepal, from where several rivers flowing into Bihar originate.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 130 missing after Indonesian passenger ship sinks in Java Sea; 107 rescued, 6 dead - video
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Indonesian rescuers intensified a search in the Java Sea for 130 people reported missing after the passenger ship Virgo Transport 8 overturned and san.
articles.body: Indonesian rescuers intensified a search in the Java Sea for 130 people reported missing after the passenger ship Virgo Transport 8 overturned and sank in bad weather.At least 107 people were rescued and six bodies recovered after the vessel, carrying 243 people including 213 passengers and 30 crew members, lost contact with authorities early on Sunday.The ship had departed Surabaya in East Java on Saturday for Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, said the vessel’s captain had reported rough seas, with waves reaching up to three metres, before sending a distress message.“The ship’s operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather,” Sudayana said in a video briefing.The captain had reported that the vessel was listing before authorities received information that it had overturned and subsequently sunk, officials said.The Banjarmasin search and rescue agency said it received a report about two hours after contact with the ship was lost at around 2am on Sunday. The vessel’s last known position was about 148 kilometres from a pier in Banjarmasin.Search teams were deployed to the area, supported by four vessels, including a navy ship, as well as a helicopter. Nearby tugboats and other vessels also assisted in the rescue operation.By Sunday afternoon, rescuers had brought 107 people to safety and recovered six bodies, Sudayana said. The rescued passengers were transported on different vessels, with some expected to be taken to a port in East Java.Hundreds of relatives gathered at Banjarmasin’s Trisakti port command centre, checking passenger manifests and rescue lists as authorities continued efforts to locate those still missing.The Japanese-built Virgo Transport 8 was designed to carry both passengers and vehicles. Officials cautioned that the manifest figure may not reflect the actual number aboard, as passenger numbers on Indonesian ferries can differ from official records.Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for inter-island travel. Maritime accidents remain a recurring concern, with safety enforcement frequently under scrutiny.The latest incident comes days after a ferry fire in the Philippines killed at least 76 people and left others missing. The latest accident follows another Indonesian ferry disaster last month, when at least 211 people were rescued from a vessel that caught fire in rough seas near Bali; one died and four remained missing. The incident happened less than two weeks after another Indonesian ferry, the Mutiara Sentosa 2, caught fire in waters off the main island of Java, leaving at least five people dead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Road to key Yemeni city reopened after Houthis advance along Red Sea
articles.summary: A main access road to the city of Taiz in south-western Yemen has been reopened following an advance by Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the country's western...
articles.body:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have captured the key port city of Mokha in Taiz province, giving them control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline.

Government forces still control parts of Taiz province, including the capital city of the same name, but fighting in the area continues with reports of attacks on Houthi positions.

The conflict in Yemen, involving Iran and Saudi Arabia, has left over 150,000 people dead from fighting and another 220,000 from indirect consequences, with 22 million people currently dependent on humanitarian assistance.

A main access road to the city of Taiz in south-western Yemen has been reopened following an advance by Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the country's western coast, local government and military sources reported on Sunday.

The Houthis now control the country's entire Red Sea coastline after capturing the key port city of Mokha in Taiz province from government forces earlier this week.

Mokha is located some 90 kilometres west of the city of Taiz. Government forces currently still control parts of Taiz province including its capital city of the same name, but fighting in the area continues.

Military sources said that government forces had again attacked Houthi positions in the Taiz area. Houthi-owned television channel Al-Masirah reported that Saudi Arabia had bombed targets to support pro-government forces.

According to Houthi-controlled news agency Saba, the Iran-backed rebels attacked weapons depots and command centres in Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government for more than a decade. A 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, but also with little prospect of an end to the war.

Fighting has flared up again amid the wider war involving Iran, plunging the already impoverished country, which borders Saudi Arabia and Oman, deeper into civil war.

According to UN estimates from 2021, more than 150,000 people were killed in fighting, while another 220,000 died as a result of indirect consequences of the war, including hunger and disease. Around 22 million people in Yemen currently depend on humanitarian assistance.

Their recent advance along the country's western coast will allow the Houthis to ramp up attacks and blockades on shipping launched amid resurging tensions with Saudi Arabia.

A Houthi spokesman said that shipping would remain safe, with the exception of Saudi vessels.

articles.title: Russia strikes truck near Polish border in western Ukraine
articles.summary: Europe News: Russia attacked a truck near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, Polish and Ukrainian officials said, in the latest strike near Nato territory as .
articles.body: Russia attacked a truck near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, Polish and Ukrainian officials said, in the latest strike near Nato territory as Moscow and Kyiv intensify long-range attacks.The attack took place about 800 metres from Poland, briefly disrupting operations at the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing, Polish border guards told Reuters. The crossing later resumed operations.Russia’s defence ministry said it had targeted infrastructure used to facilitate military cargo shipments from Europe into western Ukraine. Ukraine relies on its borders with Poland, Romania and Moldova for trade and arms supplies.Russia has targeted Ukrainian border crossings with Western allies in recent weeks as both sides increasingly focus on disrupting each other’s economic and military infrastructure more than four years into the war.In the Russian-controlled part of southeastern Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, the head of Russia’s state nuclear energy company Rosatom accused Ukraine of striking fuel trucks near the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, Europe’s largest.Russia has controlled the plant since March 2022. It remains close to the front line. A Ukrainian military spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.In Russia, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk in the Volga region of Tatarstan said Ukrainian drones had struck “civilian and industrial” targets in the city, killing at least two people and injuring several others.Mayor Radmir Belyaev did not specify which targets were hit. Nizhnekamsk is home to a major oil refinery that has been targeted in previous attacks.Ukrainian authorities did not immediately comment on the Nizhnekamsk strike but said they had struck another refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
